questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent blistering on the dorsal surfaces of the hands and feet triggered by minor trauma, along with severe photosensitivity. Genetic testing reveals mutations in the FERMT1 gene. Which of the following statements about Kindler Syndrome is correct?
opts: It is an autoimmune-mediated blistering disorder with positive autoimmune serology and HLA associations
It represents a structural defect involving loss of kindlin-1, a focal adhesion protein linking actin filaments to the extracellular matrix
It is classified as a subtype of Junctional Epidermolysis Bullosa with cleavage exclusively within the lamina lucida
It demonstrates autosomal dominant inheritance with complete penetrance in all affected individuals
questions.exp: Kindler Syndrome is a primary genetic disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in FERMT1, resulting in absent kindlin-1 protein that normally mediates focal adhesion between basal keratinocytes and the extracellular matrix. It is NOT an autoimmune disease and is autosomal recessive, not dominant. Unlike other EB subtypes, Kindler exhibits mixed-level skin cleavage rather than cleavage confined to a single ultrastructural plane.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with a 3-week history of asymptomatic linear papules on the left forearm. The eruption follows Blaschko lines and consists of 1-3mm flat-topped, skin-colored papules arranged in a continuous band. Histology shows a band-like superficial lymphocytic infiltrate with a characteristic deep perivascular and periadnexal infiltrate embracing eccrine glands and hair follicles. Which immunological mechanism best explains the pathogenesis?
opts: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity directed against basement membrane collagen
CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte attack on aberrant epidermal keratinocyte clones expressing novel membrane antigens
Th2-skewed immune response with IgG immune complex deposition
Neutrophilic infiltration triggered by complement-mediated leukotrienes
questions.exp: Lichen striatus is pathogenically driven by CD8+ T-cell-mediated immune response against aberrant clones of epidermal keratinocytes. Following a trigger (viral infection, trauma, or vaccination), mutated cells express novel membrane antigens that become targets of cytotoxic CD8+ lymphocytes, resulting in the characteristic interface dermatitis with apoptotic keratinocytes and perivascular infiltrates.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine CD8+ KILLER CELLS (CTLs) storming a STRIPED CASTLE—each tower (aberrant clone) gets ATTACKED after a VIRAL TRIGGER breaches the gate, leaving a SINGLE UNILATERAL STREAK of destruction on the armory (extremity).

questions.q: A pregnant woman at 12 weeks gestation is diagnosed with primary syphilis. She receives adequate penicillin treatment. Based on Kassowitz Law and fetal immunocompetence, what is the expected outcome regarding fetal infection?
opts: Fetal infection is almost always prevented because treatment occurs before 16–18 weeks and before full fetal immunocompetence develops
Fetal infection occurs despite treatment because T. pallidum crosses the placenta as early as 9–10 weeks
Fetal infection is prevented only if treatment is given before 9–10 weeks of gestation
Fetal infection will develop with benign stigmata because the mother has primary syphilis
questions.exp: Adequate maternal penicillin treatment before the 16th to 18th week of pregnancy almost always prevents fetal infection because the fetus does not achieve full immunocompetence until 18–20 weeks of gestation. Before this immunocompetence threshold, characteristic inflammatory tissue destruction cannot occur, allowing maternal treatment to prevent infection before irreversible stigmata develop. 🏰 Palace: Imagine a PENICILLIN SHIELD erected around the CASTLE FETUS at week 12, holding strong until week 18 when the BABY KNIGHT finally gains armor (immunocompetence)—the window closes after week 16–18.

questions.q: A newborn presents with discrete, non-blanching, dark blue violaceous macules and papules (2–10 mm) distributed across the trunk and extremities at birth. Biopsy shows poorly circumscribed aggregates of nucleated erythroid precursor cells, immature leukocytes, and megakaryocytes within the dermis without true inflammation. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains this "blueberry muffin" sign?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of dermal fibroblasts mediated by anti-type IV collagen antibodies
Cutaneous extramedullary hematopoiesis (EMH) occurring in response to profound fetal systemic stress
Vasculitis of the superficial and mid-dermal blood vessels with leukocytoclasis
IgA-mediated immune complex deposition within the dermal vasculature
questions.exp: The blueberry muffin sign represents a distinct morphological reaction pattern of cutaneous extramedullary hematopoiesis, where the undifferentiated dermal mesenchyme reverts to embryonic hematopoietic function in response to severe fetal stress such as infection, anemia, or bone marrow replacement. This is not an autoimmune, immunobullous, or primarily genetic disease. The histology characteristically shows nucleated blood cell precursors without true inflammation or vasculitis.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture the dermal mesenchyme as a MEDIEVAL BLACKSMITH reverting to FORGING BLOOD in the castle basement when the royal blood factory (bone marrow) fails—EMH is the skin's emergency backup hematopoietic forge.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy with a history of atopic dermatitis presents with poorly defined, round hypopigmented macules on his cheeks that fail to tan despite summer sun exposure. Histology shows mild spongiosis with lymphocyte exocytosis, hyperkeratosis, and follicular plugging. Which of the following best explains the hypopigmentation in pityriasis alba?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes by pathogenic autoantibodies targeting tyrosinase
Low-grade eczematous dermatitis disrupting melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes, possibly worsened by Malassezia-derived dicarboxylic acids inhibiting tyrosinase
HLA-linked genetic predisposition resulting in selective melanocyte apoptosis in the epidermis
Neoplastic transformation of sebaceous gland epithelium leading to secondary hypopigmentation
questions.exp: Pityriasis alba is fundamentally a low-grade localized eczema and post-inflammatory hypopigmentation condition, not an autoimmune or neoplastic disorder. The hypopigmentation results from eczematous inflammation disrupting melanosome transfer, compounded by potential inhibition of tyrosinase by serum copper deficiency or Malassezia dicarboxylic acid metabolites. There is no specific target autoantigen, pathogenic autoantibody, or HLA association.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CASTLE with FOLLICLES (hair towers) where MELANIN BOXES are blocked from being DELIVERED by EczemaGoblins, while MALASSEZIA ACID DEMONS pour TYROSINASE POISON through the hallways—chaotic warehouse logistics, not immune war!

questions.q: A 3-month-old infant presents with a deep, ill-defined reddish-blue plaque on the neck that has rapidly enlarged over 2 weeks. Laboratory investigations reveal thrombocytopenia (45,000/μL), elevated D-dimer, and prolonged PT. Which vascular tumour is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
opts: Infantile haemangioma (GLUT1-positive)
Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma
Congenital haemangioma (RICH type)
Pyogenic granuloma
questions.exp: Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma (KHE) is the prototypical locally aggressive vascular tumour that uniquely triggers Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon—a consumptive coagulopathy causing thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenaemia, and elevated D-dimer. In contrast, GLUT1-positive infantile haemangiomas never cause KMP, making this immunophenotypic distinction clinically critical. The deep, ill-defined, infiltrative presentation extending into the subcutis and beyond is characteristic of KHE rather than the superficial tufted angioma variant.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 3] Kaposiform Haemangioendothelioma and Tufted Angioma

questions.q: A 3-week-old infant presents with widespread, asymptomatic streaky hyperpigmented macules following a V-shaped pattern on the back and S-shaped pattern on the chest. There is no history of preceding vesicles or inflammation. Histology shows increased melanin in basal keratinocytes with normal melanocyte numbers and no dermal melanophages. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
opts: Hypomelanosis of Ito with dermal involvement
Linear and Whorled Nevoid Hypermelanosis (LWNH)
Segmental vitiligo with secondary repigmentation
Inflammatory erythema multiforme with post-inflammatory changes
questions.exp: LWNH presents in early infancy with diffuse, streaky hyperpigmented macules following Blaschko's lines (V-shapes on back, S-shapes on trunk), lacks preceding inflammatory stages, and shows epidermal melanotic hypermelanosis without dermal melanophages. The normal melanocyte count with increased basal keratinocyte melanin is pathognomonic. This is caused by postzygotic somatic mutations affecting melanin production in keratinocytes during early embryogenesis.

questions.q: A 2-month-old infant born to a mother with systemic lupus erythematosus develops permanent conduction abnormalities on cardiac imaging. Which specific cellular target of maternal autoantibodies accounts for this irreversible cardiac manifestation of neonatal lupus?
opts: Sodium-potassium pumps on ventricular myocytes
L-type calcium channels on fetal cardiomyocytes
Mitochondrial membrane proteins in the sinoatrial node
Gap junction proteins in the atrioventricular node
questions.exp: Cardiac neonatal lupus erythematosus is the most severe manifestation, occurring in 61% of NLE patients, and is caused by anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies that specifically target L-type calcium channels on fetal cardiomyocytes. Unlike other cutaneous manifestations of NLE which are transient, cardiac injury is permanent because of direct targeting of the cardiac conduction system, particularly the atrioventricular node.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle's HEART chamber, imagine CALCIUM (Ca) LOCKS (L-type channels) on tiny baby CARDIOMYOCYTES—the evil anti-Ro/SSA MOTHER THIEVES pick these locks, stealing the baby's heartbeat FOREVER (irreversible), while her skin owl-eyes fade away with time.

questions.q: A carrier mother with X-linked recessive Menkes disease shows patchy hypopigmentation along Blaschko's lines on her trunk and neck, but remains clinically asymptomatic. Which cellular mechanism best explains her localized skin findings?
opts: Functional somatic mosaicism (lyonization) resulting in random X-chromosome inactivation
Haploinsufficiency of the ATP7A gene in heterozygous females
Incomplete penetrance of the mutation in carrier females
Compensatory upregulation of ATP7B gene on chromosome Xq21
questions.exp: Female carriers of X-linked recessive Menkes disease are typically asymptomatic due to protective heterozygosity, but may display focal skin manifestations including swirled patches of hypopigmentation and hair abnormalities along Blaschko's lines. This occurs due to functional somatic mosaicism from random X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization), where patches of cells expressing the mutant ATP7A allele show defective copper transport and impaired tyrosinase function.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a FEMALE CARRIER standing at the castle's CROSSROADS where two GLOWING X-CHROMOSOMES battle—one SHUTS DOWN randomly in each cell patch (lyonization), creating STRIPED BLASCHKO WALLPAPER of pale hypopigmented LINES like a ZEBRA's stripes painted on her skin.

questions.q: A 4-week-old neonate presents with profuse, purulent nasal discharge that is blood-tinged and highly infectious. The mother received no antenatal care. Which of the following best describes this clinical finding and its significance in congenital syphilis?
opts: Snuffles (syphilitic rhinitis), often the first symptom of early congenital syphilis, representing active spirochetal infection
Acute viral rhinitis secondary to neonatal immunodeficiency from congenital syphilis
Bacterial superinfection of the nasal mucosa unrelated to Treponema pallidum
Congenital nasal stenosis mimicking infectious rhinitis in early syphilis
questions.exp: Snuffles is a characteristic early manifestation of congenital syphilis, typically appearing in the first weeks of life with profuse, watery discharge that becomes purulent and blood-tinged, and is teeming with spirochetes. It represents one of the earliest clinical signs of early congenital syphilis and indicates active, overwhelming infection. 🏰 Palace: Picture a baby's SNOUT running like a FOUNTAIN (snuffles) in week 3–4, with spirochetes SWIMMING in BLOODY PUS—the infectious hallmark of early congenital syphilis.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate born to a mother with no prenatal care presents with blueberry muffin lesions, sensorineural deafness on audiometry, and periventricular intracranial calcifications on cranial ultrasound. Which congenital infection is most likely responsible for this clinical triad?
opts: Congenital rubella syndrome (with patent ductus arteriosus)
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) with periventricular calcifications
Congenital toxoplasmosis (with diffuse/tram-track calcifications)
Congenital syphilis (with periostitis)
questions.exp: CMV is the most common viral cause of blueberry muffin baby today and characteristically presents with sensorineural deafness and strictly periventricular (not diffuse) intracranial calcifications. Rubella causes cataracts and PDA; toxoplasmosis causes diffuse/tram-track calcifications and chorioretinitis; congenital syphilis presents with different systemic manifestations.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A CYTOMEGALOVIRUS (CMV) with a GIANT EYE wearing EARPHONES sits inside the PERIVENTRICULAR CASTLE WALLS—CMV = big virus + big deafness + peri-ventricular calcifications, the toxic triad.

questions.q: A 6-week-old neonate presents with erythematous, annular patches on the face and periorbital area, giving a characteristic appearance that prompts the parents to ask why their baby looks like an owl. Which maternal autoantibody is present in >90% of cases of cutaneous neonatal lupus erythematosus?
opts: Anti-La/SSB antibodies
Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies
Anti-U1-RNP antibodies
Anti-dsDNA antibodies
questions.exp: Cutaneous neonatal lupus erythematosus is caused by maternal IgG1 autoantibodies directed against ribonucleoproteins, with anti-Ro/SSA present in >90% of cases. The classic presentation features arcuate, polycyclic, or annular lesions on the face and scalp with a predilection for periorbital areas, creating the characteristic 'owl eyes' or 'raccoon eyes' appearance.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a mother OWL perched on a RO (Ro/SSA) branch in the castle tower, >90% of the time she's there—when her babies are born, they inherit her owl-eyed stare and facial mask.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a firm, dome-shaped papule on his finger with a rough surface and pathognomonic black dots. Histopathology shows hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, papillomatosis with "church spire" projections, and prominent koilocytes in the upper stratum spinosum. Which HPV type is most likely responsible?
opts: HPV-3
HPV-1
HPV-10
HPV-28
questions.exp: Common warts (verruca vulgaris) are caused by HPV 1, 2, 4, 27, or 57, with the histological hallmark being koilocytes and "church spire" papillomatosis. The clinical presentation of a dome-shaped lesion with black dots on the hand is classic for common warts. HPV-3, 10, and 28 cause flat warts, which have a different morphology and histology.

questions.q: A 3-month-old male infant presents with sparse, depigmented hair resembling steel wool, doughy pale skin, and developmental regression with seizures. His parents report he appeared normal at birth. Which gene mutation is responsible for this clinical presentation?
opts: ATP7A gene on chromosome Xq13.3
FGFR3 gene on chromosome 4p16
KRT5 gene on chromosome 12q13
COL7A1 gene on chromosome 3p21
questions.exp: Menkes disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7A gene located on chromosome Xq13.3, which encodes a copper-transporting P-type ATPase. This mutation prevents copper export from intestinal cells, resulting in systemic copper deficiency and failure of copper-dependent enzymes including lysyl oxidase, tyrosinase, and cytochrome c oxidase. The classic presentation with steel wool hair and neurodegeneration at 2-3 months of age is pathognomonic for Menkes disease.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a COPPER PUMP (ATP7A) stuck in the castle's INTESTINAL GATE at chromosome XQ13.3—copper piles up INSIDE like a traffic jam, starving the kingdom of trace element treasure, turning HAIR to STEEL WOOL and BRAINS to SCRAMBLED EGGS.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with a well-demarcated, irregularly bordered tan-brown patch on his left shoulder that has been present since early childhood. During puberty, coarse dark terminal hairs have erupted over the lesion, and he has developed acneiform lesions confined to the affected area. Which genetic mutation and pathophysiological mechanism best explains the androgen-driven evolution of this lesion?
opts: ACTB gene mutation causing postzygotic somatic mosaicism with potentiated Hedgehog pathway signaling in pilar smooth muscle cells
FGFR3 gene mutation with constitutive activation of fibroblast growth factor signaling in basal keratinocytes
KIT gene mutation with altered melanocyte migration and survival during neural crest development
PTEN gene mutation leading to loss of negative regulation of phosphoinositide 3-kinase pathway in sebaceous glands
questions.exp: Becker's nevus is driven by postzygotic somatic mutations in the ACTB gene encoding beta-actin, which potentiate Hedgehog pathway signaling and primarily affect pilar smooth muscle cells in the dermis, disrupting hair follicle and pilar muscle development. The androgen receptor hypersensitivity and increased density within lesional skin explains the puberty-driven hypertrichosis and acneiform eruptions over the patch. The condition follows a paradominant inheritance pattern, occurring almost always sporadically as a mosaic trait.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: ACTB mutations march like ACTIN SOLDIERS through the HAIR BARRACKS (pilar smooth muscle), waving HEDGEHOG FLAGS—when ANDROGEN BELLS ring at puberty, they unlock HYPERTRICHOTIC CHAOS and ACNE EXPLOSIONS.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 6-month history of small, red-brown papules on his trunk and proximal arms. Each papule is capped with a tightly adherent, micaceous scale that reveals a shining brown surface when gently scraped. There is no scarring. What is the predominant T-cell phenotype driving the pathogenesis in this condition?
opts: CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells with minimal CD4+ involvement
CD4+ helper T-cells, some expressing FoxP3 regulatory phenotype
B-cells producing pathogenic autoantibodies against dermal antigens
Th17 cells predominantly secreting IL-17 and TNF-α
questions.exp: Pityriasis Lichenoides Chronica is T-cell-mediated, with the pathogenic infiltrate predominantly composed of CD4+ helper T-cells rather than CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells (which predominate in PLEVA). Notably, some PLC T-cells express FoxP3, a regulatory T-cell marker, which may explain the more indolent chronic nature of lesions. PLC is not autoantibody-mediated and requires no humoral autoimmune component.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a FORT (FoxP3) guarding FOUR-LEAFED CLOVERS (CD4+) in the castle keep—calm sentries maintaining order, preventing the chaos of CD8+ ASSASSINS (acute PLEVA) who would destroy the kingdom.

questions.q: An 8-year-old child with Kindler Syndrome who presented with severe acral blistering and photosensitivity in infancy now shows marked improvement in blister formation and sun sensitivity. However, the parents report progressive development of mottled skin changes, widespread skin thinning, and a distinctive 'cigarette paper-like' appearance on the hands and feet. What is the name of the characteristic skin pattern reflecting this pathological evolution?
opts: Erythema multiforme with progressive scarring
Poikiloderma with progressive cutaneous atrophy
Xeroderma pigmentosum with solar elastosis
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita with dermal scarring
questions.exp: Kindler Syndrome demonstrates a characteristic temporal evolution in which the blistering tendency and photosensitivity paradoxically improve by age 8, while progressive poikiloderma (mottled hyper- and hypopigmentation with telangiectasia) and widespread cutaneous atrophy develop and persist lifelong. The acral surfaces develop pathognomonic 'cigarette paper-like' atrophy, distinguishing this phase from the initial neonatal blistering presentation.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with widespread hypopigmented patches exceeding 2 cm in diameter affecting her trunk and limbs, with fine white scale. This clinical presentation differs from classic pityriasis alba in several ways. Which statement accurately distinguishes the extensive variant from classic pityriasis alba?
opts: Extensive PA affects children aged 4–8 years, while classic PA favors teenagers and young adults

Extensive PA shows larger lesions (>2 cm) with widespread trunk and limb involvement, and demonstrates female preponderance in teenagers and young adults, whereas classic PA favors facial involvement in younger children
Extensive PA is caused by autoimmune mechanisms targeting sebaceous glands, while classic PA results purely from post-inflammatory changes
Extensive PA exhibits complete absence of sebaceous glands histologically, whereas classic PA shows normal sebaceous gland architecture
questions.exp: The extensive (generalized) variant of pityriasis alba is characterized by larger lesions (typically >2 cm), widespread distribution beyond the face involving trunk and limbs, and predominantly affects teenagers and young adults with female preponderance. Classic pityriasis alba presents as smaller facial patches (0.5–3 cm) primarily in childhood. Both variants share the same pathogenic mechanism of low-grade eczematous inflammation, not autoimmunity.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: In the GIRLS' TOWER (teenage girls), GIANT BLOTCHES (>2cm) spread across the WHOLE CASTLE BODY—the throne room AND barracks covered in POWDER SNOW. The CHILD'S FACE TOWER shows only tiny SPOTS—a stark contrast of scale and distribution!

questions.q: Pigmentary mosaicism represents a spectrum of genetically determined anomalies caused by postzygotic somatic mutations occurring early in embryogenesis. Which of the following characteristics is INCORRECT regarding the pathophysiology and inheritance pattern of these conditions?
opts: Over 90% of chromosomal aberrations overlap with known pigmentation genes
Lesions are typically confined to the epidermis, specifically basal layer keratinocytes and melanocytes
These conditions follow autosomal dominant inheritance patterns with high penetrance in offspring
Both sexes and all races are affected, with contrast easier to detect in darker skin phototypes
questions.exp: Pigmentary mosaicism conditions are strictly sporadic and NOT inherited, as they result from somatic postzygotic mutations occurring after fertilization in a single cell line. Therefore, they do not follow autosomal dominant or any Mendelian inheritance pattern. All other statements accurately reflect the pathophysiology: epidermal localization, high overlap with pigmentation genes, and universal susceptibility across demographics.

questions.q: A mother brings her 8-year-old child with a 2-month history of a unilateral linear band of 1-2mm papules on the right leg that has been gradually resolving. She is concerned about permanent scarring. Which statement accurately distinguishes nail lichen striatus from nail lichen planus?
opts: Nail lichen striatus causes permanent pterygium scarring; nail lichen planus causes only reversible dystrophy
Nail lichen striatus is restricted to a single nail on the affected extremity with focal matrix damage, while nail lichen planus can cause permanent pterygium formation
Nail lichen striatus always affects multiple nails; nail lichen planus affects only one nail
Both conditions cause identical dystrophy patterns with equal scarring risk
questions.exp: Nail lichen striatus is extremely rare and usually restricted to a single nail on the affected extremity. Because the matrix damage is focal and follows a Blaschko line, dystrophy is restricted to only the medial or lateral portion of the nail plate. Unlike nail lichen planus, which can cause permanent scarring (pterygium formation), nail lichen striatus does not cause permanent scarring.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: In the NAIL TOWER (striatus), only ONE NAIL WINDOW breaks along a LIGHTNING BOLT (Blaschko), leaving TEMPORARY CRACKS. Across the moat in PLANUS CASTLE, the entire fortress crumbles into PERMANENT PTERYGIUM RUINS.

questions.q: A 10-year-old girl presents with a segmental patch of hyperpigmentation on her trunk showing an irregular, jagged outline resembling an archipelago of islands. The lesion exhibits a pseudo-Darier's sign when rubbed. Which statement accurately characterizes the epidemiological and structural features of this presentation?
opts: The patient's presentation is atypical because Becker's nevus shows a male predominance of 5:1 to 6:1 in isolated cases, though the sex ratio reverses in syndromic variants
The archipelago pattern and pseudo-Darier's sign indicate transition to melanoma, requiring immediate excisional biopsy
The hyperpigmentation is caused by a true melanocytic nevus with increased melanin-producing cells in the stratum basale
This represents an autoimmune condition with circulating anti-melanocyte antibodies driving the pigmentary abnormality
questions.exp: Becker's nevus shows a profound male predominance of 5:1 to 6:1 in isolated presentations, though this sex ratio remarkably reverses in syndromic variants. The characteristic archipelago-like jagged outline and pseudo-Darier's sign (temporary firming and elevation from localized smooth muscle contraction) are benign diagnostic features. The condition is not a true melanocytic nevus, lacks melanocyte proliferation, and is not autoimmune—it is an organoid hamartoma affecting epidermis and dermis.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: In the BOY'S CASTLE (5:1 male ratio), ARCHIPELAGO ISLANDS jut from the sea of skin—rub the magic patch and PSEUDO-DARIER'S GOOSEBUMPS rise as SMOOTH MUSCLE SOLDIERS contract—SAFE treasure, not MELANOMA monsters!

questions.q: A 9-year-old girl has multiple small, flat-topped, flesh-colored papules arranged in linear streaks on her shins that appeared after scratching. She also has similar lesions on her face and dorsal hands. Histology shows basket-weave hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and "bird's eye" appearance with prominent koilocytes but absent papillomatosis. What is the name of this characteristic clinical phenomenon?
opts: Köbner phenomenon
Pseudo-Koebner phenomenon
Isomorphic response
Blaschko's phenomenon
questions.exp: Flat warts (verruca plana) characteristically exhibit the pseudo-Koebner phenomenon, arranging themselves in linear streaks along scratch marks or trauma lines. This distinguishes flat warts from other wart types and is a key diagnostic clinical feature. The true Köbner phenomenon involves new lesions at trauma sites in conditions like psoriasis.

questions.q: Which of the following statements best explains why kaposiform haemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma are now regarded as existing along a single biological spectrum rather than as separate disease entities?
opts: They have identical ISSVA classification as locally aggressive tumours
They share overlapping histology, identical immunophenotype, and the unique capacity to trigger Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon
Tufted angioma invariably progresses to kaposiform haemangioendothelioma within 2 years
Both lesions are GLUT1-positive and demonstrate rapid spontaneous involution
questions.exp: The unifying spectrum concept is supported by three key overlapping features: (1) inappropriate proliferation of both blood and lymphatic endothelial cells in both lesions; (2) identical immunophenotype; and (3) shared capacity to cause the life-threatening Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon. The distinction between them lies in depth and aggressiveness—tufted angioma represents the superficial, indolent end while KHE represents the deep, locally aggressive end of the same biological process. This shared biology sharply separates both from GLUT1-positive infantile haemangioma, which never causes KMP.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 3] Kaposiform Haemangioendothelioma and Tufted Angioma

questions.q: A 5-year-old girl with pityriasis lichenoides chronica on the trunk is being investigated for possible systemic disease. Serological testing for autoimmune markers (ANA, complement levels, anti-dsDNA) is ordered. What is the expected result?
opts: Strongly positive ANA with low C3/C4 levels indicating active autoimmune disease
Positive anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies confirming dermal-epidermal junction autoimmunity
All negative—no pathogenic autoantibodies or complement activation occur in PLC
Positive rheumatoid factor with circulating immune complexes
questions.exp: PLC is strictly a T-cell-mediated (cellular immune) disease with no humoral autoimmune component. There are no pathogenic autoantibodies, no targeted host autoantigens, and no complement-mediated injury. Serological markers for autoimmune disease will be negative, which critically distinguishes PLC from true autoimmune blistering disorders and connective tissue diseases.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A SERUM MOAT (negative serology) surrounds the castle—no antibodies storm the gates, only CELLULAR GUARDS (T-cells) patrol inside; the castle's defense is PERSONAL, not HUMORAL.
